title: The story inside the story (Mark 5:21–43)
hook: Mark sandwiches the bleeding woman inside Jairus's daughter; both are daughters

segments.voice: Yesterday, Legion: a man freed and sent home. Your line was go home and tell. Today Jesus crosses back.

A father falls at a teacher's feet, begging him to come: his little girl is dying. They set off through a pressing crowd, and every minute counts. And then the teacher stops. Mark does something you saw on day two hundred: he starts one story, stops it halfway, tells a whole second story in the middle, and only then finishes the first. Scholars call it a Markan sandwich. And the two stories turn out to be mirrors of each other.
screen: `A FATHER BEGS: COME QUICKLY.` → `THE TEACHER STOPS.` → `A MARKAN SANDWICH.`

segments.voice: First, the outside story. Jairus, a leader of the synagogue, an important man, falls at Jesus's feet. My little daughter is dying, he says; come and lay your hands on her. Jesus goes, and the crowd presses in around him. Second, the inside story. In that crowd is a woman who has been bleeding for twelve years. She's spent everything on doctors and only got worse, and under the law the bleeding also kept her ritually unclean. She thinks: if I can just touch his clothes. She does, and she feels it: she's healed. And Jesus stops. "Who hath touched my garments?" The disciples point out the obvious: the whole crowd is pressing on you. Meanwhile Jairus stands there, his daughter dying, and Jesus waits. The woman comes forward, trembling, and tells him the whole truth. He says: "Daughter, thy faith hath made thee whole: go in peace." Third, the bad news. While he's still speaking, messengers arrive: your daughter is dead; why trouble the master any further? Jesus turns to Jairus: "Fear not, only believe." At the house, he takes the girl by the hand and says: talitha cumi. Mark keeps the words as Jesus said them, then translates: damsel, arise. She gets up and walks, and Jesus tells them to give her something to eat. Fourth, the mirrors. The woman has been sick twelve years; the girl is twelve years old. Both are called daughter. Both are unclean by the law, one bleeding, one dead. She touches him; he takes the girl by the hand. And the interruption that looked like it cost the girl her life turns out to be part of the same healing.
screen: `JAIRUS: MY DAUGHTER IS DYING.` · `A WOMAN TOUCHES HIS GARMENT.` · `FEAR NOT, ONLY BELIEVE.` · `TWELVE YEARS, TWO DAUGHTERS.` · then, large: `DAUGHTER, THY FAITH HATH MADE THEE WHOLE.`

segments.voice: Think back over the last day or two: who stopped you on your way somewhere? A child with a question, a coworker at your desk, a text from someone who needed to talk; pick one, and ask what they actually needed. If you pray, hold that person before God and ask to see the next interruption differently; if you don't, picture yourself stopping for them, the way Jesus stopped.
Talitha cumi. Aramaic for little girl, arise: Jesus's words to Jairus's daughter. Today's word.
Your line: interruptions are the ministry. Jesus stopped, and the girl still rose. That's two hundred five.

howItsDone: Catholics hear the raising of Jairus's daughter and the healing of the woman at Sunday Mass in Ordinary Time (Year B), and the Church prays for the sick through the sacrament of anointing.

original.note: Aramaic, written in Greek letters: little girl, arise; Mark keeps Jesus's own words.

trapdoor: what you thought: two separate miracles.
what it means: one story inside another, two daughters mirrored, and the interruption becomes part of the healing.
what a scholar hears: intercalation, the Markan sandwich; talitha koum preserved in Aramaic.
recall: a day set apart to stop and rest
moved with compassion, from the gut

sources.quoted: Daughter, thy faith hath made thee whole: go in peace

notes: Douay-Rheims Mark 5:30, 5:34 and 5:36 given from memory; confirm.
Talitha cumi: Douay spelling 'Talitha cumi'; Aramaic transliterated here in Greek letters as ταλιθα κουμ (manuscripts vary: κουμ / κουμι). Confirm.
Ritual impurity of a woman with a flow of blood (Leviticus 15:25–27) and of a corpse: stated carefully as 'unclean by the law', not as social contempt; a Jewish reader should check the framing.
